plan: Literary narrative of about 590 words (CLD-P-ACT-R-000014) under the batch-13 lessons: keys avoid paraphrasing a single sentence, two hard items connect distant paragraphs, the drawer's meaning is tested in one item only.

passages.title: Others
passages.text:
The sign had been in the window for three weeks before my grandfather admitted that it meant what it said. CLOSING AT THE END OF THE MONTH, it read, in my mother's neat capitals, and every morning he walked past it to unlock the door as though it were a notice for someone else's shop. Customers came in to say they were sorry. He thanked them, took their watches, and wrote out repair tickets with dates two and three weeks away, some of them later than the last day of the month.

My mother had asked me to spend my Saturdays there, helping him decide what would be sold and what would be thrown out. I was fifteen and had my own ideas about how Saturdays should be spent, but I went. The shop was narrow and smelled of oil and brass. Along the back wall stood a cabinet of shallow drawers, each one labeled in his small, slanting hand: mainsprings, crowns, crystals, and one drawer, near the bottom, labeled simply "Others."

"What goes in Others?" I asked on the first Saturday.
"Things that don't fit," he said, and went back to his bench.

We did not sort much that day, or the next. He would hand me a box of parts and tell me to separate the good from the bad, and when I held up a gear and asked which it was, he would take it from me, turn it under the lamp, and begin explaining how it had been cut, by whom, and in what year, until the afternoon was gone and the box was still full. I began to suspect that the sorting was not really the point, though I could not have said what the point was.

In the third week a woman came in with a pocket watch that had belonged to her father. My grandfather opened the case, held it to his ear, and told her it needed only a cleaning. He did the work while she waited, and when she tried to pay, he waved the money away. After she left, he stood at the window for a long time with his back to me, and I pretended to be busy with the box of gears.

On the last Saturday of the month, the shop was quieter than I had ever heard it. The repair tickets had been called in, the watches returned, and the cabinet stood half empty. My grandfather sat at his bench with nothing on it. I opened the drawer labeled "Others" at last. Inside were not parts but tickets, dozens of them, yellowed, for watches that had never been collected. Each had a name and a date, some forty years old, and on each, in the same slanting hand, he had marked the repair as finished.
"Why did you keep these?" I asked.
He looked at the drawer for a while before he answered. "Somebody might come back," he said.

I did not tell my mother about the drawer. When we carried the cabinet out to her car that evening, I made sure the bottom drawer stayed shut, and when she asked whether there was anything in it worth keeping, I said I would go through it myself.

candidates.stem: Taken together, the repair tickets the grandfather writes in the first paragraph and his answer "Somebody might come back" in the sixth paragraph suggest that he:

choices.A: still expects the shop to be rescued before the end of the month.
choices.B: is careless about dates and the details of his customers' orders.
choices.C: struggles to accept that the shop and its work are coming to an end.
choices.D: wants customers to pay in advance for repairs he will not finish.

candidates.evidence: some of them later than the last day of the month
candidates.explanation: He books repairs past the closing date and keeps decades-old tickets in case owners return. Both show a reluctance to let the work end, even after admitting the shop will close.

A.rationale: The first sentence says he finally "admitted that it meant what it said."

B.rationale: He labels drawers neatly and keeps tickets for forty years; carelessness does not fit.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests he takes payment, and he marks repairs as finished.

hints: What do both details have in common?
Does the passage say he denies the closing, or only that he has trouble with it?

strategy.explanation: Find what links the two details.

candidates.remember: Synthesis questions: name what two distant details share.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires combining details from the first and sixth paragraphs; choice A is tempting but contradicted by the opening sentence.

candidates.stem: When the narrator says she "began to suspect that the sorting was not really the point" (paragraph 4), she most nearly means that she sensed:

choices.A: the Saturdays mattered to her grandfather for some reason other than clearing the shop.
choices.B: her grandfather secretly hoped to train her to take over the shop as a watchmaker someday.
choices.C: her mother had invented the whole task mainly to keep her busy on her weekends.
choices.D: her grandfather could no longer tell good parts from worn ones.

candidates.evidence: though I could not have said what the point was
candidates.explanation: Little sorting gets done because the grandfather turns each part into a story; the narrator senses the time serves him in some other way she cannot name.

B.rationale: She says she "could not have said what the point was"; becoming a watchmaker is never suggested.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the mother's motive was to keep her busy.

D.rationale: He explains each part in detail, showing expert knowledge.

hints: Does the narrator know what the real point is?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that claim more than she knows.

candidates.remember: When a narrator "could not have said," avoid choices that name a specific motive.

candidates.stem: The description of the drawer labeled "Others" in paragraphs 2 and 3 mainly serves to:

choices.A: show how carefully the grandfather organized the parts he used for repairs.
choices.B: set up a small mystery that the narrator resolves near the end of the passage.
choices.C: hint that the narrator will someday inherit and reopen the shop.
choices.D: explain why the shop was no longer able to stay in business.

candidates.evidence: I opened the drawer labeled "Others" at last
candidates.explanation: The odd label and the grandfather's vague answer raise a question that is answered in paragraph 6, when the narrator finally opens the drawer.

A.rationale: The labeled drawers show care, but the "Others" drawer matters because of what it turns out to hold.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the shop will reopen.

D.rationale: The drawer has nothing to do with why the shop closed.

hints: When is the drawer opened, and what is inside?

strategy.explanation: Trace the drawer through the passage.

candidates.remember: Early unexplained details often pay off later.

candidates.stem: The narrator's actions in the final paragraph most strongly suggest that she:

choices.A: plans to sell the old tickets to collectors as valuable antiques.
choices.B: fears her mother will be angry that the drawer was not emptied.
choices.C: intends to track down the owners named on the tickets and return their watches to them.
choices.D: wants to keep her grandfather's private attachment from being treated as clutter.

candidates.evidence: I made sure the bottom drawer stayed shut
candidates.explanation: After learning what the drawer meant to her grandfather, she keeps it shut and hidden from her mother, who was deciding what was "worth keeping."

A.rationale: Nothing suggests the tickets have monetary value or that she plans to sell them.

B.rationale: No sign of her mother's anger appears; the narrator offers to deal with the drawer herself.

C.rationale: The passage never says the uncollected watches are still in the shop.

hints: What did the narrator learn about the drawer just before this?
Why might she not want her mother to judge its contents?
candidates.remember: Motive questions: connect an action to what the character has just learned.

author_checklist.hardness: Requires connecting the final action to the meaning of the drawer revealed earlier; D is tempting because the tickets are for real watches.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, who wrote the sign in the shop window?
candidates.explanation: The sign was written "in my mother's neat capitals."

A.rationale: The drawer labels are in his hand; the sign is in the mother's "neat capitals."

B.rationale: The narrator never says she wrote the sign.

D.rationale: No customer is described writing anything.

candidates.remember: Detail questions: the answer is stated in the passage.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a phrase in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 6, the phrase "called in" most nearly means:
candidates.explanation: The tickets had been "called in" and "the watches returned": owners had come to claim their repairs.

B.rationale: This is the familiar meaning; the tickets were redeemed, not phoned.

C.rationale: Tickets cannot be summoned for questioning.

D.rationale: The watches were returned, which shows the tickets were claimed, not canceled.

hints: What happened to the watches at the same time?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice in the sentence.

candidates.remember: Use the next phrase in the sentence to fix the meaning.

candidates.stem: The grandfather's habit of explaining how each gear "had been cut, by whom, and in what year" (paragraph 4) suggests that he:

choices.A: cannot tell which parts are still good enough to sell.
choices.B: values the history and craft behind the parts he has handled.
choices.C: considers the narrator too young to be trusted with the parts.
choices.D: is preparing to write a history of watchmaking in the region.

candidates.evidence: begin explaining how it had been cut, by whom, and in what year
candidates.explanation: Turning each gear into a story about its making shows how much the craft and its history mean to him.

A.rationale: His detailed knowledge shows he could easily tell good parts from bad.

C.rationale: He hands her the box himself; he takes parts back to explain them, not to keep them from her.

hints: What does he do instead of simply sorting?
candidates.remember: Characterization: infer values from what a character chooses to do.

candidates.stem: The passage is narrated from the point of view of:

choices.A: the grandfather, looking back on the end of his career.
choices.B: the narrator's mother, describing her father's shop.
choices.C: an outside observer who knows every character's thoughts.
choices.D: a granddaughter recalling a time when she was fifteen.

candidates.explanation: A first-person narrator speaks of "my grandfather" and "my mother" and says "I was fifteen," looking back.

C.rationale: The narrator uses "I" and does not know her grandfather's thoughts.

candidates.remember: Point of view: check who says "I" and when.
